Handles mass (g), volume (ml) and count families, including us/metric pairs (lb, oz, kg, gal, qt, cup, tbsp, tsp, ml, l)
Cross-dimension conversion (ml to g) succeeds only when the item supplies a density or a per-item conversion in unit_conversions; otherwise returns unknown with a reason
Item-specific conversions win over generic ones (a can of this product resolving to a mass)
Never throws and never silently returns a number for an unconvertible pair; unknown is a value, not an exception
Unit tests include the moveCheckedToPantry case: 2 gal added to a pantry row measured in fl oz converts rather than landing in a mismatch list
npm run test:run passes
userStories.notes: src/lib/canonicalUnits.ts + src/lib/canonicalUnits.test.ts (27 tests, all passing). Exports toCanonical(quantity, unit, item) returning {value, unit, via} | {unknown: true, reason}, plus isUnknown() narrowing and sumCanonical() for folding several amounts. BUILT ON THE EXISTING LAYER, not beside it: src/lib/unitNormalize.ts (US-287, 69 tests) already did generic mass/volume/count/package normalisation, so this imports normalize() and adds only what the ledger needs - per-item conversions, density, and a typed unknown. unitNormalize.ts is unmodified and its 69 tests still pass. Criterion 2 asserted across both dimension families: kg/lb/oz/g into grams (1 lb and 16 oz agree within 0.5 g) and l/gal/qt/cup/tbsp/tsp/fl oz plus the half-gallon token into millilitres. Criterion 6 asserted directly as its own test: 2 gal and 256 fl oz both resolve to 7570.82 ml and are equal, so the moveCheckedToPantry case that currently lands in mismatchedNames simply converts. Criterion 4 asserted twice - a package unit (2 can -> 800 g via item_conversion) which nothing generic can do, and a collision case where the item says a cup of this flour is 120 g and that beats the generic 236.588 ml. Conversion keys go through the same tokeniser as units, so "Fl Oz" in unit_conversions matches "fl oz" on input. Criterion 3 asserted: ml->g returns unknown with reason /without a density/ unless density_g_per_ml is present; with 1.42 it gives 142 g from 100 ml and inverts correctly; densities of 0, -1 and NaN are refused rather than divided by. count<->mass explicitly does NOT accept a density, because how much a piece weighs is per-item and belongs in unit_conversions. Negative quantities ARE accepted, deliberately - a debit is a negative movement. Also covered: items with no declared canonical_unit classify from the unit itself (lb->g, cup->ml, dozen->count), which is what the US-669 backfill needs; and purity, asserting the item object is not mutated and results are referentially transparent. Criterion 1 note: the return type carries an extra via field (item_conversion | generic | density | identity) beyond the shape in the criterion, so callers and tests can assert WHICH rule fired rather than only the number. userStories.title: Item resolver with confidence and provisional items
userStories.description: As a parent, I want the app to know that the thing on my receipt is the thing in my pantry so that my list and my stock stop disagreeing.
acceptanceCriteria: New src/lib/itemResolver.ts exports resolveItem(input: { text, barcode?, householdId }, ctx: { aliases, items, canonicalProducts }): { itemId, confidence, matchedBy } | { provisional: true, proposedName, confidence }
Resolution order is exactly: barcode exact, household alias exact on normalized text, household alias fuzzy above threshold, canonical_products seed, propose new
matchedBy identifies which step won, so callers and tests can assert the path rather than only the outcome
Below the confidence threshold it returns provisional rather than guessing; the threshold is a named exported constant, not a literal at a call site
Follows merged_into_id: resolving to a merged item returns the surviving item's id
Pure: context is passed in, nothing is fetched inside

userStories.notes: src/lib/itemResolver.ts + src/lib/itemResolver.test.ts (26 tests, all passing). Exports resolveItem(input, ctx), plus isProvisional() narrowing, similarity(), resolveMergeRedirect() and the named constant FUZZY_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD = 0.82. Criterion 7 covered with at least one test per step: (1) barcode exact, including that it beats an alias which would have matched the text, and that whitespace around the barcode is ignored; (2) alias exact, including that plurals and unit prefixes all reach the same item through normalizeItemText, and that the alias own confidence is carried rather than assumed to be 1; (3) alias fuzzy, asserting "chiken breast" resolves to chicken breast above threshold while "chicken thigh" does NOT (different purchase), that a low-confidence alias never lends more confidence than it has, and that the BEST alias wins rather than the first over the line; (4) canonical_products seed by name and by barcode, and that it loses to a household alias; (5) propose new. Criterion 3 asserted throughout via matchedBy (barcode | alias_exact | alias_fuzzy | canonical_product | none). Criterion 4: the threshold is exported and has its own test asserting a typo scores above it and a different cut of meat scores below it. Criterion 5 (merge redirect) has 5 tests: an alias pointing at a merged row returns the survivor, a multi-hop chain a->b->c resolves to c, a cycle stops rather than looping (MAX_MERGE_HOPS plus a seen-set), a self-pointing row is stable, and an id absent from the list is returned unchanged. They are distinguished by matchedBy and by whether a seed of category/defaultUnit/defaultAisle/barcode is attached. That is a deviation from criterion 1 literal shape, which implies matchedBy only on the resolved branch; the provisional branch carries it too so the caller can tell a recognised-but-uncreated item from a genuinely unknown one. proposedName is deliberately the cleaned ORIGINAL text, not the sorted normalized form, so a new pantry row is never called "breast chicken". acceptanceCriteria: BEFORE UPDATE trigger on foods detects a quantity change that did not originate from the US-667 mirror and appends a correction movement whose delta is new minus current canonical balance

Writes from a null quantity to a value are treated as a correction from zero, not an initial movement
Concurrent updates are safe: the correction is computed against the row's locked current value, not a stale read

userStories.notes: supabase/migrations/20260901000004_kitchen_loop_direct_write_translation.sql + supabase/tests/us668_direct_write_translation.test.sql (committed, since this is the riskiest object in the epic and the evidence belongs in the repo). VERIFIED BY EXECUTION on a disposable postgres:16-alpine container with all five kitchen-loop migrations applied in filename order; torn down afterwards, production never touched. CRITERION 1 DEVIATION, deliberate and evidenced. The criterion specifies a BEFORE UPDATE trigger. That does not work here and Postgres says so in its own words. A BEFORE trigger that appends a movement fires item_stock -> the US-667 mirror -> an UPDATE of the very row whose UPDATE has not yet returned, and Postgres raises: "tuple to be updated was already modified by an operation triggered by the current command", with the hint "Consider using an AFTER trigger instead of a BEFORE trigger to propagate changes to other rows." I built exactly that shape first to confirm it rather than argue it, and the client write was silently lost: foods.quantity stayed 0 after being set to 5. Implemented as AFTER UPDATE OF quantity with a WHEN (OLD.quantity IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.quantity) clause. Everything else in criterion 1 is met: the delta is the client new value in canonical units minus the current ledger balance. Criterion 2 (re-entrancy) met, and broken twice on purpose. The mirror sets app.kitchen_loop_mirror (transaction-local) while it writes foods.quantity and this trigger stands down when it sees it; independently, the mirror UPDATE carries WHERE quantity IS DISTINCT FROM display_value, so once the two agree it writes nothing at all. Asserted by Case 2: a new-client movement produces exactly ONE movement, with no correction echoed back, and by criterion 6 below. Criterion 3 met and asserted explicitly: every test item starts with quantity NULL, and the first direct write produces reason=correction with zero rows of reason=initial. `initial` belongs to the US-669 backfill alone; using it here would make a parent edit indistinguishable from seeded history. Criterion 4 (concurrency) met, asserted with TWO REAL SESSIONS rather than by reasoning. Session A began a transaction, set quantity to 10 kg and held the row lock for three seconds; session B attempted 20 kg on the same row and blocked. Result: A appended +10000, B appended +10000 (20000 minus A committed 10000), final stored 20000 = folded 20000 = foods.quantity 20. A stale read would have made B append +20000 and left the balance at 30000. The serialization point is the foods row lock, which concurrent writers take before reaching the trigger; the SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on item_stock covers the case where a movement arrives by another path. Criterion 5 met: supabase/tests/us668_direct_write_translation.test.sql covers all four named cases. Case 1 old-client write: correction +5000 with display_quantity 5 and display_unit kg recorded alongside. Case 2 new-client movement: quantity reads 1 gal, exactly one movement. Case 3 interleaved, which is the case that matters most - old client sets 2 kg, a NEW client cooks 500 g, old client sets 3 kg, producing the history correction +5000, correction -3000, cook -500, correction +1500, with stored = folded = 3000 and foods.quantity = 3. The third write correctly computed its correction against a balance a different client had changed in between, which is the entire purpose of this trigger, and the intermediate cook is still in the history rather than overwritten. Case 4 no-op: repeating the same value and updating an unrelated column both append nothing (count stays 4). Criterion 6 met: total movements across the whole suite is 5, bounded and small, and the mirror guard flag reads empty after every statement. No recursion in any case. Also asserted beyond the criteria: an opaque display unit round-trips one-to-one (6 servings <-> 6 count), an unconvertible write appends NOTHING rather than guessing (honey stocked in ml and displayed in g produces 0 movements and leaves the written value alone for rpc_stock_mirror_divergence to surface), and the US-666 reconcile invariant reports 0 drifting items across all of it. Added public.to_canonical(), the inverse of US-667 from_canonical(), with the same per-item-conversion precedence and the same opaque-unit-over-count rule. MIGRATION ORDER DEPENDENCY FOUND while testing: 20260901000003 (legacy mirrors) depends on public.ladder_rung_index from 20260901000000 (merge items), because SQL function bodies are validated at creation. Applying 000001-000004 without 000000 fails partway through 000003, and because psql autocommits each statement the earlier objects in that file DO get created - so the mirror installed while the is_safe rollup did not, and a careless run would have looked mostly fine. Real deployment applies in filename order so this is not a defect, but a partial apply of that file leaves a half-installed state worth knowing about. Torn down afterwards; production never touched. Criterion 1 met: 8 initial movements written, one per stocked item, each converted from its display unit. Not skipped, because a skipped row reads as zero stock and a household would open the pantry to find everything gone; not guessed into grams, because that number would be wrong and would look right. BATCHING CAVEAT recorded in the migration header: Supabase applies each migration file in a transaction, so a DO block cannot COMMIT between batches and the in-migration loop does not actually shorten the lock window. That is why the work is a callable function - on a large database an operator calls it repeatedly OUTSIDE a transaction, which is what genuinely keeps locks short. userStories.notes: src/lib/inventoryLedger.ts + src/lib/inventoryLedger.test.ts (218 tests passing: 18 unit tests plus 200 property seeds). Criterion 1 met: exports foldMovements(movements) and applyMovement(state, movement), plus applyAll, balanceOf, unitOf, emptyLedger, foldExcludingReversals and ledgerAnomalies. CRITERION 2 DEVIATION, deliberate, and this is the discrepancy flagged in US-666 notes. The criterion says reversals are excluded from the balance along with the movement that reversed them. The SERVER does not do that: apply_inventory_movement_to_stock() adds every delta it sees, and a reversal is an ordinary row whose delta negates the original, so the pair cancels. The two rules agree whenever a reversal is an exact negation, which rpc_reverse_movements_by_ref guarantees. They differ only on malformed data, and then summing still agrees with item_stock while excluding silently does not - which would surface as phantom drift in the US-666 reconciliation, a report whose whole value is being trustworthy. There is a second reason, arguably the stronger one: reversed_by_id points at a row that may not be in the set being folded. Page a household history and an original can arrive without its reversal. Excluding on the back-pointer then drops the original and keeps nothing to cancel it, producing a wrong number that looks like a small one rather than an obvious error. Asserted directly: for a page containing only a reversed original, summing gives -450 (correct for that page) and excluding gives 0. Rather than quietly pick one, BOTH are implemented and their equivalence is asserted. foldExcludingReversals() implements criterion 2 literally and is exported so the two can be compared; every one of the 200 property seeds asserts they produce identical balances on well-formed data, and two hand-written tests assert the same for single and multi-item reversals. A third asserts they diverge when a reversal is not an exact negation, which is the case criterion 2 was really trying to protect against - and ledgerAnomalies() reports that row as unbalanced_reversal instead of absorbing it into a balance. Criterion 3 met: order-independence asserted over all 24 permutations of a four-movement sequence, and again on every property seed against a shuffled copy. Applying the same id twice is a no-op, asserted both by balance and by identity (the second applyMovement returns the SAME state object, not a copy). Duplicates inside one fold count once however many times they appear, and a replayed offline queue reaches the same balance as a clean one. Criterion 4 met: 200 deterministic property seeds, each generating 5-30 movements across three items with reversals and duplicated rows, asserting fold equals sequential apply, equals a shuffled fold, and equals the excluding rule. A seeded PRNG is used rather than Math.random so any failure is reproducible from the seed alone. Criterion 5 met: verified by grep - no supabase, Date, fetch, readFile, process or localStorage reference - and by two tests asserting neither the state nor the movements array is mutated. A BUG IN MY OWN PROPERTY GENERATOR, found by the test failing and worth recording because the first read was misleading. 200 seeds failed initially and it looked like a module defect. It was not: the generator duplicated rows FIRST and then reversed the copies independently, producing one logical movement id carrying two different reversals - a history the server cannot create, since a second reversal overwrites reversed_by_id. fold and applyAll agreed on every item on every seed throughout, so criterion 4 was never actually in doubt; only the excluding-rule comparison diverged, and it diverged because the data was malformed. The generator now assigns reversals first and appends exact clones afterwards, and the malformed shape has its own explicit test. Also caught and corrected: the comment on that new test originally claimed the excluding rule lands 8.48 away from the server, while the assertion showed both rules agreeing. Both rules DO agree there, because a second reversal overwrites the back-pointer so only one is ever pointed at. An inaccurate comment beside a passing test is worse than none, so it was rewritten to say what is actually asserted. Type note: ledgerAnomalies iterates a deliberately widened Partial<LedgerMovement>. isUsable is a type predicate, so narrowing on its negation against an already-typed value collapses the failing branch to never and the reported fields become unreachable - that cost 3 errors against the ratchet before it was restructured. Gates: typecheck-ratchet 1182 = baseline (1185 before the narrowing fix), lint-ratchet 1229 = baseline, inventoryLedger 218/218. SUITE HEALTH, worth raising separately: the full run reported 7 failures this iteration against 3 last iteration, with no change on my part that could touch them. Run in isolation, storageBucketScanner passes, resolveChromium passes 11/11, and one of the two storageBucketPolicies failures passes - leaving only the known pre-existing functionTreeBuckets (US-643) and storageBucketPolicies images-bucket (US-635). Several tests in this suite fail intermittently under full-suite parallel load and pass alone: resolveChromium, SEOManager, storageBucketScanner and one storageBucketPolicies case.
